technique: letting one plain object carry the feeling
lesson:
Today we work on one technique. It's letting a single plain object hold the feeling, so you don't have to state the feeling outright. This poem picks one thing and keeps returning to it. It opens "The jar of bitters stands on the sill where you set it." Then it tells you what's inside: "the gentian and ginger / gone to work in the dark." Later it names why you'd want it: "that clean burn / a man reaches for when the cold gets honest." The jar does the work. You never get told the person is tired or alone, but the jar sitting there, waiting, makes you feel it.

Here's why that works. A real object gives your attention something to hold. You trust it because it's specific, and the feeling comes in under the object instead of being announced.

Try this: pick one real object the person owns, and let the poem keep coming back to it.

The second time, listen for how often the jar and the cold return.

Here is the poem, twice.
poem:
The jar of bitters stands on the sill where you set it,
amber behind glass, the gentian and ginger
gone to work in the dark the way slow things do.
You bought it for the throat, that clean burn
a man reaches for when the cold gets honest—
and the cold got honest this week, a run of nights
that put four frosts down and locked three hard,
the low places skinned with ice thin as a held word.
Last night let up some, came in soft at thirty-seven,
the mildest of the string, the ground given a little grace.
You've spent your days tending the far ends of other lives,
a bed aired for a stranger, a door left right for him.

The kitchen's yours first thing—
coffee, a warm pan, nobody to answer to but the morning. Rise and have it.
